summary: A survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers from August 1974, showing how far sites had come in implementing the new Telnet protocol. It is a status snapshot. It is updated by RFC 702.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the first planned monthly report on new-protocol Telnet servers. It records what the survey found at ARPANET server sites in August 1974.

questions: which hosts supported new telnet in 1974
subtitle: The first survey of new-protocol Telnet servers on ARPANET, as of August 1974.

tldr.problem: A new Telnet protocol was being introduced, and the report records which server hosts had implemented it.
tldr.mechanism: A survey program and manual checks gathered server behavior as seen by the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA on August 15, 1974.
tldr.outcome: 10 of 32 server hosts had a new-protocol implementation. The unit metadata says RFC 702 updated this report.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The author presents this as the first of planned monthly reports on new-protocol Telnet implementations at server hosts on the ARPA Network. The report covers server Telnets only. It assumes new-protocol user Telnets at TENEX sites running TENEX 1.32, but makes no broader claim about user implementations.

The author reports that less than one-third of server sites had a new-protocol server, about a month after TENEX 1.32 was released.
sections.plainLanguage: This report checks server programs only. The author says fewer than one-third of the surveyed sites had the new protocol running.

sections.title: Summary Counts
sections.content:
Of 32 server hosts, 10 had a new-protocol implementation, 19 had none and three had unknown status because they were down to the network. Among the ten implementations, five used the new protocol on socket 27 and the old one on socket 1; four used the new protocol on both sockets; and one used it only on socket 1.

The author says only half of the sites with a new-protocol server used the logger socket conventions correctly, according to his understanding. The report identifies the first group as operating correctly by his reading.
sections.plainLanguage: 10 of 32 hosts had a new-protocol server. The survey could not reach three hosts, and 19 had no new-protocol server.

sections.title: The Host Table and Options
sections.content:
The table lists each host number and name, what runs on socket 1 and socket 27, and implemented new-protocol options. OLD and NEW identify the protocol, X means there is no server at the socket, and a question mark means unknown status.

I# means the server implements option # incoming to the user, while O# means outgoing from the user. The listed options are 0 Transmit-Binary, 1 Echo, 3 Suppress-Go-Ahead and 6 Timing-Mark. A note marks SU-AI as giving an improper response to a request for option 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The table gives one row per host and shows the protocol and options found at each socket. The report explains the symbols used in those columns.

sections.title: How the Survey Was Done
sections.content:
The author gathered data with a survey program run at various times and added a few manual checks. The results show server behavior as seen by the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA on August 15, 1974; surveys from other sites may differ.

The report notes that some servers marked as new-protocol on socket 1 actually try to communicate with both old- and new-protocol users, depending on the control sequences they receive.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers describe what one survey saw from BBNA on one date. Another survey could report different results.
